title.en: Monotone relaxation, settling and rejected negative weights

summary: Verify that tentative distances only decrease, settled values never improve, and precondition violations are rejected.
objective: Every applied relaxation follows the declared update policy, no settled distance improves later, and non-finite or negative weights are rejected.
applies_when: A shortest-path algorithm is stepped or animated with visible tentative values.
The graph weights are editable by the viewer.
The implementation may leave stale entries in its priority queue.
intent_signals: what happens with a negative edge
example_prompts: Check the relaxation steps and preconditions in this shortest-path scene.

principles: Tentative distances only decrease. Strict improvement is the declared update policy of this implementation rather than a theorem, since updating a predecessor on an exact tie can also yield a valid shortest-path tree; a policy that updates on ties must then guard against cycles among zero-weight edges.
Settling depends on nonnegative weights, so a negative weight is a precondition violation to reject explicitly rather than a case to render silently.
Duplicate priority-queue entries are an implementation choice; if they are used, the stale entry must be skipped when dequeued and that skip should be visible in the trace.
implementation: Log each relaxation attempt with the edge, the old and new tentative values, and whether the update was applied.

Check non-increasing distance sequences. Under strict-improvement policy every applied update decreases distance; under a declared tie-update policy an equal-distance predecessor change must preserve the equal path cost and an acyclic predecessor graph, with the deterministic tie rule recorded.
Record the dequeue order with the settled distances and confirm that no settled vertex is improved afterwards.

Reject nonfinite or negative edge weights. For each relaxation from a finite reachable distance, also check that the candidate path sum is representable before comparing or committing it; report out-of-range cost separately from unreachable, or use a validated numeric representation/input bound that prevents overflow. Exercise negative weights, zero-weight ties and a finite-edge case whose sum exceeds the supported range.
observable_checks: Every applied relaxation matched the declared update policy and updated distance and predecessor in the same step; under a strict-improvement policy an update with equal values identifies a non-strict comparison, and under a tie-updating policy the predecessor graph is additionally checked for cycles.
No settled distance improves later in the run, and unreachable vertices keep an infinite value rather than a large finite one.

Negative, not-a-number and non-finite weights are all rejected with a message naming the edge, and zero-weight ties resolve by the declared policy so repeated runs give the same tree without a predecessor cycle.

known_limits: Checks the invariants of the declared nonnegative-weight algorithm; graphs with negative weights need a different algorithm and a different check.
Authored verification guidance; no algorithm was executed for this record.
creative_affordances: Adapt the scenario, scale and presentation to your subject; this record fixes what must be checked, not how the scene must look.

claims.statement: Relaxing an edge tests whether the best known path to a vertex improves by going through another vertex and updates the data structures if so, and the algorithm that repeatedly adds the non-tree vertex with the lowest distance requires nonnegative weights.
claims.scope: Edge-weighted digraphs with nonnegative weights as described in the cited section.

source_refs.locator: Edge relaxation definition and Dijkstra algorithm with nonnegative weights
